production.note: Calendar years, from Evo's title 'Ferrari Enzo (2002 - 2004)' and 'the Enzo, launched in 2002'. Ferrari: unveiled at the 2002 Paris Motor Show; 'Just 399 examples were planned: a 400th would follow and was donated to the Vatican for charity' (ferrari-magazine-enzo). Hagerty: 'with only 400 built (80 of which were designated for the U.S. market)' and lists the US car as a 2003 model (hagerty-enzo). Market: the car was sold in the US, but no Ferrari figures stated for the US market could be opened, so the record uses Ferrari's own metric rating and a European magazine's panel throughout, with calendar build years, rather than mixing markets.

body.note: Two-seat, mid-engined fixed-roof car; no open version was sold.

configuration.note: Spec panel: 'Engine | V12, 5998cc' (Ferrari F140 engine, mid-mounted)

displacementL.note: 5,998 cc. Also carsales (Peter Robinson, 2002): '92mm bore and 75.2mm stroke give a capacity of 5998cc' (carsales-enzo-2002).

aspiration.note: 'its naturally aspirated, 650bhp 8500rpm V12'; Ferrari: 'the world's most powerful naturally aspirated engine' (ferrari-magazine-enzo).

fuel.note: Not stated in so many words; petrol V12, no hybrid system.

drivetrain.note: Spec panel: 'Transmission | Six-speed semi-automatic, rear-wheel drive'

transmission.note: Ferrari: 'A new six-speed automated manual gearbox gave lightning-fast shift times of just 150 milliseconds'. Evo: 'Six-speed semi-automatic' (evo-enzo). This is Ferrari's paddle-shift 'F1' gearbox; no conventional manual was offered.

powerHp.note: Quote (Ferrari): "Dry weight was just 1255kg, astonishingly light for such a powerful (660 hp) V12-powered supercar." Ferrari's 660 is a metric figure (660 cv = 485 kW; carsales' 2002 review gives '485kW at 7800rpm', carsales-enzo-2002), so it is converted: 660 x 0.98632 = 651 hp. Evo's spec panel prints the same rating as "Max power | 650bhp @ 7800rpm" (evo-enzo).

weightLb.note: Single configuration (coupe, 6-speed F1 gearbox). Quote (Evo spec panel): "Weight (kerb) | 1480kg". 1,480 kg x 2.20462 = 3,263 lb. Ferrari's own page gives only a dry weight: "Dry weight was just 1255kg" (ferrari-magazine-enzo). A lower kerb figure of 1,365 kg appears in Top Gear's auto-filled data panel (topgear-enzo-data); see discrepancies and reviewNotes. Hagerty gives 3,230 lb for the US car (hagerty-enzo).

sources.title: Ferrari Enzo (2002 - 2004) – review, history and specs of an iconic hypercar

discrepancies.reason: Dry vs kerb, and three different kerb figures. 1,255 kg is Ferrari's dry weight. 1,365 kg is the kerb weight widely attributed to Ferrari, but it was found only in auto-filled data panels and spec databases, not on a Ferrari page that could be opened. 1,480 kg is the kerb weight in Evo's editorial specification panel. Hagerty's overview of the US-market 2003 car says 'At a curb weight of 3,230 pounds' without attribution.
discrepancies.resolution: Used 1,480 kg: it is the only kerb weight from a source that qualifies under the guide (a major magazine's specification panel, labelled kerb). Auto-filled panels do not count, and Hagerty's figure is a single unattributed mention. Flagged for review in case a Ferrari document stating a kerb weight is found.

discrepancies.reason: Unit conversion. Ferrari's 660 is metric horsepower (cv); 485 kW is 650 bhp and 660 cv converts to 651 hp at the guide's factor.
discrepancies.resolution: Used 651 hp: Ferrari's 660 cv converted at 1 PS = 0.98632 hp, as the guide prescribes.

reviewNotes: Weight: 3,263 lb (1,480 kg) is Evo's specification-panel kerb weight and is the only qualifying kerb figure found. Ferrari's claimed kerb weight is widely given as 1,365 kg (3,009 lb), but only auto-filled panels and databases state it; ferrari.com's specification table could not be read (only article text is returned) and the Ferrari page that could be opened gives a dry weight (1,255 kg) only. If a Ferrari press kit or brochure stating 'kerb weight 1,365 kg' can be opened, the guide's order (manufacturer first) would make that the figure. Market: recorded as EU with calendar years because no US-market Ferrari figures could be opened; the car was sold in the US. The full range of US model years could not be sourced (Hagerty lists a 2003 model).
